title: One lock for every path to the balance

blocks.text: `synchronized` gives two guarantees: **mutual exclusion** and **visibility** (an unlock happens-before the next lock of the **same** monitor). The page's pitfalls show how both are lost: locking a different object on one path, synchronizing writes but not reads, and locking on something that is not a `private final` monitor. It also notes that a `synchronized` block always releases its monitor when an exception leaves it.

items: `deposit(long amount, Runnable whileLocked)` adds `amount` to the balance, then runs `whileLocked` **while still holding the lock** (an audit hook; tests use it to hold the lock open);
`withdraw(long amount)` takes `amount` off the balance, or throws `IllegalStateException` when the balance is smaller, leaving the balance unchanged;

blocks.text: Every one of them must use one and the same lock, so that no thread ever sees or changes the balance while another thread is inside a deposit.

rows: a `balance()` from another thread while a deposit's hook runs
waits until the deposit leaves its lock

cases.says: Deposits and withdrawals keep the balance, and a withdrawal beyond it is refused and changes nothing.
Reading the balance takes the same lock, so it waits while a deposit is inside its critical section.
A withdrawal locks the same monitor as a deposit, not a different one such as the class object.
A withdrawal that throws still releases the lock, so another thread can deposit afterwards.

concepts: Locking different objects gives neither mutual exclusion nor happens-before, and a static synchronized method locks the Class object, not the instance.
A monitor should be a private final reference, so every thread locks the same object.
A synchronized block releases its monitor even when an exception leaves it.
synchronized gives both mutual exclusion and visibility: an unlock happens-before the next lock of the same monitor.
